title: Why data centers are at the center of the Big Tech backlash
summary: Journalist Paris Marx unpacks his new book "Hyperscale."
text:
In his new book “Hyperscale,” journalist Paris Marx investigates the impact of data centers and generative AI, taking readers inside the data centers themselves and explaining how computing infrastructure that goes back decades recently became a political landmine.
The book is well-timed, to put it mildly, as data center backlash seems to have been one of the motivators for the massive blue wave seen in the recent midterm elections. And those debates are likely to continue as Democrats wield more governmental power.
In an interview with TechCrunch, Marx described the data center buildout as “fundamentally unsustainable” and “completely out of line with a livable planet,” while also arguing that these facilities make for an obvious target amidst broader anger at the tech industry. After all, if a data center is being built in your community, “it’s very physical, it’s very material.”
“It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum that you’re on,“ Marx said. “You are going to feel the effects of that in your quality of life, in your power bill, potentially in your access to water, potentially in what you hear around your community, if these air conditioning units on the roofs of data centers are making a lot of noise.”
He also suggested that data center opposition is only the most visible piece of a wider movement targeting “the physical manifestations of the tech industry, […] whether it’s the opposition to Flock cameras rolling out across the United States, or the smart glasses that Meta is trying to put on people’s faces, or even the self-driving cars that Waymo is rolling out.”
During our conversation (which I’ve edited for length and clarity), Marx and I discussed data centers’ environmental impact, how tech companies are responding to community resistance, and what it’s actually like inside a data center.
I liked your description of trying to get access to the inside of a “hyperscale” data center and then eventually taking a tour [of one]. Could you talk a little bit more about what that experience was like? How did you get in? What surprised you when you actually got in?
Getting inside of a hyperscale data center was not the easiest task in the world. I spoke to some researchers who have been doing research on data centers for a number of years longer than I had, and they told me that before the generative AI moment, and before all the attention that has been put on data centers recently, that it was quite a bit easier to do so.
I sent emails to a number of companies asking if I could get inside, often didn’t get a response, other times got a no. I ended up, after visiting the outsides of some data centers in places like northern Virginia and Ireland and spots like that, I actually went down to New Zealand to go inside of a data center itself. And the thing that struck me most was the level of security.

title: Delta flights in and out of Atlanta delayed due to system outage
summary: All Delta flights in and out of Atlanta are facing significant delays on Sunday due to a problem with the system that calculates a plane's weight and balance. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport is Delta's largest hub and one of the busiest airports in the world. While only Delta is impacted at the moment, disruptions at […]
text:
All Delta flights in and out of Atlanta are facing significant delays on Sunday due to a problem with the system that calculates a plane’s weight and balance. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport is Delta’s largest hub and one of the busiest airports in the world. While only Delta is impacted at the moment, disruptions at Hartsfield-Jackson could potentially affect other airports and airlines if delays continue to pile up.
Delta flights in and out of Atlanta delayed due to system outage
Major delays for Delta come just a week after a nationwide groundstop.
The issues with Delta’s systems in Atlanta come just one week after an FAA outage led to a nationwide groundstop and thousands of canceled flights. According to The New York Times:
The system that went offline calculates the total weight of an airplane, including its airframe, fuel, passengers and their baggage. The system also allows pilots to determine the plane’s center of gravity and whether the weight is evenly distributed — data points that help ensure safe passage.
“Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation,” the airline said in a statement on Sunday.

title: GLP-1 drugs could have a surprisingly large environmental payoff
summary: GLP-1 drugs could cut food demand enough to free farmland larger than Italy.
text:
GLP-1 weight-loss medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy could affect much more than the waistlines of the people who take them. If widely used, our new research suggests these appetite-suppressing medicines could transform the global food system and free up vast areas of agricultural land.
The global food system is ultimately driven by demand. If people eat less, producers respond, affecting production, prices, trade, and how much land is needed. We used a powerful computer simulation to explore scenarios ranging from GLP-1 use concentrated in high-income countries to widespread global access.
With widespread use of these medicines among adults living with obesity, we estimate that reduced calorie intake could prevent up to 6.6 million deaths each year by 2050, while freeing up as much as 32 million hectares of agricultural land—an area slightly larger than Italy—for other uses.
The biggest effects, however, occurred when reduced calorie intake was combined with a shift toward healthier diets. In this scenario, up to 7 million deaths could be avoided each year by 2050, while around 46 million hectares of agricultural land would have become available for other uses. This suggests that alongside weight-loss medicines, we need to make healthier options more widely available, affordable, and more appealing.
The food system could respond in unexpected ways
Food systems are interconnected across countries. If demand falls in one part of the world, this can affect farming, trade, and food prices elsewhere, with consequences for people who are not taking the medications at all.
Lower demand from GLP-1 users, for instance, could make food cheaper. That sounds positive, but cheaper food could also encourage greater consumption among non-users, offsetting some of the intended benefit. The effects of widespread GLP-1 use, in other words, cannot be understood just by looking at individual patients’ weight loss. They ripple through the global food system.
It’s tempting to read these findings as an argument for putting more people on weight-loss medication. That would miss the bigger picture.

The Best Travel Adapters for Power On the Go
Featured in this article
Whether planning a country-hopping odyssey or a quick business trip, your journey will go more smoothly with the best travel adapters that allow you to safely charge all your gadgets wherever you land. After many work trips and family vacations I’ve tested several—both universal and basic options—and my favorites will work in most parts of the world.
The best adapters make great gifts for travelers and deserve a place in your carry-on, but check out our other travel guides, like the Best Travel Essentials, Best Travel Tech for Families, Best Travel Pillows, and Best USB-C Cables.
Updated November 2026: I added a Mukiya travel charger and a Mophie Travel Kit, removed some discontinued devices, and updated links and prices.
Travel Adapter Comparison Table
Travel Adapters: Your Questions, Answered
What Type of Adapter Do You Need?
There are 15 plug types in use across the world. Universal adapters tend to cover all of these types.
- Type A and Type B are used in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Japan.
- Type C is common across Europe, South America, and Asia.
- Type E and Type F are found across Europe in places like Germany, Russia, and France.
- Type G is used in the United Kingdom, Ireland, and a handful of other places.
- Type I is used in Australia, New Zealand, China, and Argentina.
Some countries are not usually covered by universal adapters, such as India (Type D), Israel (Type H), and South Africa (Type M or N). You'll need to buy specific plug adapters for those places. To avoid any surprises when you land, double-check what type you need before you travel.
If you're visiting just one destination, a basic plug adapter that caters to one plug type is all you need. For trips to multiple destinations or for frequent flyers, a universal travel adapter can prove more versatile. The universal adapters I recommend here have the bonus of including multiple USB ports for charging several mobile devices from a single outlet.
Do You Really Need a Voltage Converter?
Voltage converters are big, heavy, and expensive, and they don’t always work—so it’s probably best to avoid them. The reason you might think you need one is that the AC sockets on all of our recommended travel adapters do not convert the voltage coming from the socket. This means plugging into a UK socket will deliver 220 volts at 50 hertz, which is very different from the 120 volts at 60 hertz you can expect in the US. Don't worry! Your gear won’t get fried. You just need to make sure anything you plug into one of these universal travel adapters has something like this printed on it:
Input: 100–220V 50/60Hz
That should include most modern gadgets. If your device or charger can’t handle a variable voltage, it’s probably best to leave it at home. title: Google employees protest AI in schools policy
summary: More than 550 Google employees signed a petition to allow schools access to Search without AI. Parents and educators protested outside Google offices in 6 cities last week for the same ask.
text:

More than 550 Google employees signed a petition to allow schools access to Search without AI. Parents and educators protested outside Google offices in 6 cities last week for the same ask.
ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:
Parents and educators want Google to provide an AI-free version of the search engine for students. The backlash started after the company announced that they would not unbundle AI from their tools for education. SEQUOIA CARRILLO, BYLINE: Hi.

And I actually spoke to some people who pointed me towards two court cases earlier this year. Google got those dismissed by arguing that AI Overview and their search function are one tool. And those dismissals might mean that breaking them up could potentially be legally difficult for them. And when I talk to Google, they would not give us comments. So who is to say right now?
SCHMITZ: That's really interesting. So it sounds like Google has sort of backed itself into a legal corner on this issue, and it sounds like Google's own employees are angry about this.

title: TechCrunch Mobility: A/B testing robots vs. humans
summary: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and, now more than ever, the role AI is playing in it.
text:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and, now more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility!
Waymo pulling its robotaxis off freeways (again) and Zoox robotaxis launching on the Uber app illustrate the push and pull between progress and setbacks in the autonomous vehicle industry.
There are signs of growth. For instance, Tesla has now surpassed Waymo in Texas in the number of robotaxis registered with the state (Tesla has 1,507 and Waymo has 1,345). But does that translate to market dominance?
A better metric, if we’re trying to gauge who is leading, would be commercial driverless miles. And if we’re measuring cost-efficiency, another useful metric would be driverless miles per vehicle. By those measures, Waymo is still ahead, based on data available to me. But with Waymo’s recent freeways setback and Tesla’s push to expand its robotaxi fleet with Cybercabs, that lead could shrink.
Not that there needs to be a winner, by the way. Transportation is deeply fragmented, and there is room for multiple players in the U.S., not to mention the rest of the world.
A/B test: humans vs. robots
A recent discussion with my Autonocast co-host Ed Niedermeyer, whose book, “Elon Take the Wheel,” comes out December 1, got me thinking about how Las Vegas could soon become a real world A/B test of sorts for human-driven vs. autonomous ride-hailing services.
Uber, as mentioned above, just added Zoox to its ride-hailing app in Las Vegas. For now, riders don’t have much of a choice. Uber customers can increase their chances of getting a Zoox robotaxi, and they can always decline a robot ride. But they can’t directly select a robotaxi. Instead, Uber riders will be matched with one if it’s available.
Uber said that will soon change. The company plans to introduce a dedicated autonomous option in its app as “availability and reliability improve,” Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said during the company’s third-quarter earnings call in November.
Las Vegas will also become the first U.S. city where riders can access two fully driverless partners through the Uber app, he said. (Hyundai’s self-driving subsidiary Motional is also an Uber partner.)
That would give Uber riders a meaningful choice: a human driver or a robotaxi, and potentially even which autonomous service to use. And it could offer a revealing look at what customers actually prefer when given that choice. Price could tip the balance, too.
It makes me wonder whether Las Vegas will become the next battleground for organized labor as robotaxis begin competing directly with human drivers.

Reddit user ShweetsStuff discovered the songs used during a Grand Theft Auto-themed section. They found several audio files with Suno metadata that pointed back to […]
text:
The Binding of Isaac: Repentance Plus has spent the last few days getting review-bombed on Steam after it was discovered that a particular segment of the game used AI music. Reddit user ShweetsStuff discovered the songs used during a Grand Theft Auto-themed section. They found several audio files with Suno metadata that pointed back to the tracks on Suno’s site.
Binding of Isaac developer removes AI music from Repentance Plus
Creator Edmund McMillen claims he ‘had no idea’ AI music was used in the latest version of Binding of Isaac.
Creator Edmund McMillen took to X to apologize and claimed he “had no idea” the in-game GTA parody used generative AI music. Adding to the drama, Valve requires developers to disclose how and when they use generative AI in the development process, and Nicalis, Inc., the studio behind Repentance Plus, doesn’t appear to have mentioned the AI music anywhere.
Within hours of the discovery, Nicalis shared on X that Repentance Plus had been updated and the generated music files had been removed. While reviews on Steam have yet to rebound, and the game is still rated as “overwhelmingly negative,” users on X seem to be giving McMillen the benefit of the doubt, likely because he’s been quite outspoken on AI in game development, calling it “uninspired and bland” in a TikTok from 2024.

title: Review: Godzilla Minus Zero joins the list of truly stellar sequels
summary: Director Takashi Yamazaki ups the ante by pitting Godzilla against one of the monster's greatest foes
text:
It’s a rare thing for a film sequel to match or even surpass its predecessor; The Godfather Part II and Terminator 2: Judgement Day are the best known examples on a pretty short list. Go ahead and add Godzilla Minus Zero to that list. Director Takashi Yamazaki’s sequel to his critically acclaimed Godzilla Minus One (2023) is everything one could want in a Godzilla movie: human pathos, great special effects, and, ultimately, two giant kaiju duking it out over who gets to destroy Japan (and eventually the world) the most.
(Spoilers for the first film below. Spoilers for Minus Zero but no major reveals until after the gallery. We’ll give you a heads-up when we get there.)
As I wrote previously, Yamazaki wanted to return to Godzilla’s filmic roots with Minus One, setting the events in postwar Japan and tapping into the monster’s symbolic representation of the Japanese perspective on the 1940s nuclear holocaust—while also incorporating all-too-human themes of guilt and redemption. That first film focused on kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), who struggled with survivor’s guilt after he failed to take action when Godzilla attacked the Japanese base on Odo Island in 1945.
Knocked unconscious, Kōichi survived and awoke to find his parents and many others were killed in the World War II bombing of Tokyo. Kōichi rebuilt a life with a woman named Noriko (Minami Hamabe) and the orphaned baby she rescued, Akiko (Sae Nagatani). But then Godzilla re-emerged, and Kōichi resolved to die fighting the monster to atone for Odo Island. Kōichi saved the day and lived to tell the tale. He reunited with Noriko, who had a strange black bruise on her neck. And we saw a chunk of Godzilla’s remains start to regenerate, leaving things open for a sequel.
Godzilla Minus One was a massive hit, both in Japan—where it remains one of the highest grossing Japanese films ever—and worldwide, racking up $116 million globally and winning an Oscar for best visual effects. Yamazaki said in interviews at the time that there had as yet been no talk of a sequel—while also hinting at future directions a sequel might explore. He later admitted it was way of planting a seed for what would become Godzilla Minus Zero.

title: Can AI really help spot Black Friday deals? We put it to the test
summary: We put four AI models to the test to see if they could save us money on a new TV.
text:
Can AI really help spot Black Friday deals? We put it to the test
- Published
Whether it's scrolling through endless choice, spotting fake reviews, or working out if a "deal" is a deal at all, Black Friday sums up a lot of online woes.
Retailers promise bargains - but the sheer number of offers can leave us feeling no closer to finding the best deal.
It's an area where generative AI products, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, have promised to help.
But are they any good at finding Black Friday deals? We had a go ourselves a week ahead of the big day.
Figures suggest relatively few UK shoppers currently go to AI tools for help.
A recent YouGov survey of 19 countries found the UK ranked second-last in the proportion of people who said they had used AI to help them shop.
Crucially, 36% of respondents who said they would be shopping around Black Friday didn't plan to use an AI tool at all.
But the survey suggested a growing number of people were considering it - and tech firms have released features to capitalise on this.
Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping for UK users in November and OpenAI launched a Shopping Research tool on ChatGPT days before last year's Black Friday.
In the US, Google recently launched Universal Cart, with AI-powered features such as price tracking and identification of relevant promo codes.
But there has been criticism that fact-checking AI ends up taking more time, while some brands are working to try to make sure their products show up in chatbot answers.
We asked four models to find a 55-inch TV deal, using the free versions of many of the most popular tools.
While this was not a rigorous scientific test, the experience we had produced mixed results.
ChatGPT - full price and not available to buy
OpenAI's ChatGPT came up with four options.
Its top pick was a Hisense TV on Chinese retailer Joybuy's website, on sale for £499 down from £649.
The next recommendation was a 55-inch TCL-branded TV, but a sidebar showed prices for the 50-inch version, from £379 to £814.
Option three was the same Hisense TV as before, but for full price at £649 from John Lewis and Richer Sounds.
This was the "best safer purchase" according to ChatGPT, as the sites offered longer guarantee periods.
But clicking on the links did not go well. Both retailers said the TV was no longer listed online.
The fourth option was equally fruitless - another TCL TV, at full price, £150 over our budget and not available online.
At the bottom, ChatGPT served one last offer - "one OLED option to compare" - for a £1,100 LG TV that was marked as "Ad".

title: Can a TV be too large? An investigation
summary: Can a TV be too large? This writer's recent upgrade to a 65-inch OLED came with some unexpected challenges.
text:
For the past couple of years, I’ve wanted to upgrade my home entertainment situation from the humble trappings of my long sufficient 55-inch TCL smart TV to the model much coveted by cinephiles the world over: the OLED.
The organic light-emitting diode is a specific monitor technology that has really changed the TV industry. Unlike an LED TV, which creates images by shining a backlight through a panel of pixels, OLEDs leverage millions of self-lighting pixels, which provides significantly better pixel control, and can generate a much more nuanced image with deeply vibrant colors and a more intense light and shadows.
In short: They look way better.
They are also significantly more expensive, which is one reason that I’ve held off on investing in one for years. However, this year I couldn’t wait any longer. I finally sprang for an upgrade and, since I was already upgrading on image quality, I decided to upgrade the size, too: I bought a 65-inch LG evo C4, which is the company’s mid-range unit released in 2024.
At first, the experience was amazing. The television rendered colors and shadows wonderfully and, seeing as one of the goals with this purchase was to indulge my physical media habit, I began running through my collection of 4K Blu-ray discs with the madcap energy of a true fanatic.
However, things took a bit of an unexpected turn when, midway through “McCabe and Mrs. Miller,” I was suddenly overcome by a wave of nausea. I’m not particularly sensitive to motion sickness, but this sensation — which made it feel vaguely like I was going to hurl — persisted for several hours after it initially began. It was then replaced by a small tension headache.
In short: Not great.
I discovered that this is actually a somewhat common experience for new OLED adopters. Indeed, Reddit is rife with posts from new television owners who claim they feel like their big new toy is breaking their brain.
“I got the tv yesterday and still feel sick today,” one Redditor, who said they had recently purchased an LG C2, wrote. “Feel light headed and nauseous a day later. Thinking about taking it back. Is this normal? I’m scared to turn the thing on lol.”
Others blamed the sheer size of the screen. One guy, who bought an 85-inch TLC, claimed it had led his wife to the conclusion that “it’s too big and say that she feels sick watching. Is that a thing that a screen can be too big?”
There doesn’t seem to be a consensus on why this happens. Many Redditors blame certain motion-smoothing settings. However, my TV did not come with those settings enabled. Others blamed viewers for sitting too close to the screen — yet I was sitting a solid nine feet away, which is well within the recommended range for a 65-inch screen.
Finally, others have argued that the screen brightness could be agitating users’ eyes. I dialed down the brightness on mine to around 50 percent, although I had doubts as to whether this actually had anything to do with the feelings I was having.

title: “Race realism” isn’t realistic—and it isn’t good science
summary: Modern genetics does not support claims of innate racial differences in intelligence.
text:
At this year’s World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, US President Donald Trump stated that people from Somalia have low IQs. “I always say these are low-IQ people,” he said in his speech. His son, Donald Trump Jr, made a similar statement about Haitian people in 2024 (Trump’s government has since ended the protected status of both Somali and Haitian migrants in the US).
These statements and their consequences are symptoms of a growing trend in Western politics: the re-emergence of racial views of human nature that have been largely in hiding for the past 70 years. Narratives about the innate intellectual inferiority of black or brown people compared with white people—which can still be found in academic journals today—are fuelling far-right propaganda in some of the world’s largest democracies. Such claims underpin misinformation strategies on social media and bolster political movements.
These narratives are sometimes euphemistically referred to as “race science” or more recently “race realism.” But, as we argue, they are not actually scientific. One member of this community, Nathan Cofnas, recently attracted public attention by accusing the late Jason Arday of plagiarism.
What got less attention was that Cofnas has links to a network of people who make supposedly scientific claims about the innate intelligence, criminality, or sexuality of different racial groups. Some within this network are affiliated with universities, giving their work the mask of legitimacy.
This group produces work that has the appearance of science, but which is methodologically deeply flawed and fails to engage with rigorous scientific research. Yet they regularly succeed in publishing this work in (a handful of) mainstream academic journals.
How do they manage to do this, and what are the consequences?
Scientific shortcomings: biology and genetics
Contemporary race scientists position themselves as persecuted but legitimate scientists who are prevented from pursuing their work for ideological reasons. They sometimes refer to what they defend as hereditarianism. This is the idea that genetic differences play a key causal role in determining differences in human behavior and intelligence between human groups—such as races—over purely environmental differences.
Yet scientific evidence has shown repeatedly and from many points of view that hereditarian thinking is both flawed and wrong. Race scientists make extremely simplistic claims such as: “Black people have innately lower intelligence than white people, because selection pressures resulted in the evolution of higher intelligence in white people.” No part of this claim can be scientifically supported; not from the point of view of genetics, evolutionary biology, or psychology.
In the 1970s, the influential evolutionary biologist Richard Lewontin famously showed that there is more genetic variation within human groups than between them. Socially defined racial groups just aren’t that genetically different from one anot

title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
summary: Pressures weighed on US markets, with the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average pushed into correction territory.
text:
Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
- Published
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.
The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.
Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.
Both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.
The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.
The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.
Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.
Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.
Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."

title: Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance
summary: Signal is limiting users' ability to take screenshots in both its Android and iOS apps.
text:
Signal announced Friday that it’s limiting users’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what President Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI.
Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”
“Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she said. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”
Signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default. Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS.
That said, users can disable this setting if they wish, which Whittaker said would “break our privacy guarantees.” She also admitted this is an “incomplete” solution, as it doesn’t “address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data.”

title: Sheherazaad’s Khudgarzi is gorgeous, ‘genre-chaotic’ South Asian folk
summary: Sheherazaad started making ripples in the music world a few years ago with her EP Qasr, which was produced by Grammy Award winner Arooj Aftab. Now she's back with Khudgarzi, her reverb-drenched folk-noir debut LP that's primarily sung in Urdu. The instrumentation on Khudgarzi draws on traditional South Asian music, including Carnatic and Hindustani styles, […]
text:
Sheherazaad started making ripples in the music world a few years ago with her EP Qasr, which was produced by Grammy Award winner Arooj Aftab. Now she’s back with Khudgarzi, her reverb-drenched folk-noir debut LP that’s primarily sung in Urdu.
Sheherazaad’s Khudgarzi is gorgeous, ‘genre-chaotic’ South Asian folk
The debut LP from Sheherazaad blends traditional Indian instruments with Western electronic flourishes and feminist narratives.
Sheherazaad’s Khudgarzi is gorgeous, ‘genre-chaotic’ South Asian folk
The debut LP from Sheherazaad blends traditional Indian instruments with Western electronic flourishes and feminist narratives.
The instrumentation on Khudgarzi draws on traditional South Asian music, including Carnatic and Hindustani styles, but also dabbles in Arabic folk traditions, as well as modern Western electronic music. Trip-hop flourishes and Spaghetti Western guitar brush up against tanbur and ghatam. Sheherazaad’s stunning voice sits atop dripping percussion and seasick drones singing about the plight of “The Selfish Woman.”
For Sheherazaad, the character of the selfish woman isn’t the villain, it’s a charge leveled at women who didn’t conform to societal norms, “eccentric women whose desire for agency was often met with an awful end.” Even if you can’t understand most of the lyrics, the atmosphere tells the story clearly enough. From the barely simmering anger of “Registaan” to the bleak repetition of “Qatil” and the fantastical yearning of “Zeher,” Khudgarzi is clearly the work of a woman exploring what it means to be a woman, the lasting legacy of colonialism, and the perpetual threats of a patriarchal society.
Khudgarzi is alternately a funeral dirge and a celebration of femininity. Sheherazaad owes a lot of the album’s ability to navigate these various themes and moods to her impressive production work, top-notch mixing by J. Valleau, and the cast of over 30 “genre-chaotic” virtuosic musicians including Ria Modak, Sarathy Korwar, Jay Chakravorty, Shunya, and Qasim Naqvi. The instrumentation never distracts, though. It’s not showy, and all emulsifies around Sheherazaad’s vocals in a shawl that feels equal parts comforting and oppressive.
Khudgarzi is available now on Bandcamp and most major streaming platforms, including YouTube Music, Spotify, Apple Music, Deezer, and Qobuz.

title: NASA’s new Moon plan is taking shape, but some big questions remain
summary: "We tend to have a lot of technical discussion and debate. That point will continue to be debated."
text:
SpaceX's Starship returns to Starbase, Texas, on November 14, 2026, one day after launching from the same location atop a Super Heavy booster.
Credit:
SpaceX
SpaceX's Starship returns to Starbase, Texas, on November 14, 2026, one day after launching from the same location atop a Super Heavy booster.
Credit:
SpaceX
SpaceX’s successful recovery of its Starship rocket last weekend cleared a major hurdle on NASA’s path to the Moon, opening up possibilities for higher launch rates and an all-important, long-delayed orbital refueling demo next year.
For SpaceX’s purposes, Saturday’s mid-air rocket catch will help engineers learn how to rapidly reuse Starships. That should expedite SpaceX’s deployment of its newest generation of Starlink Internet satellites. NASA, meanwhile, believes a higher launch cadence will lead to faster learning as SpaceX develops a deep space version of Starship to ferry astronaut crews to the surface of the Moon.
Early next year, SpaceX plans to bring online a second Starship launch site at Kennedy Space Center, Florida. A second Starship factory is also under construction at Kennedy, joining SpaceX’s existing SpaceX production line at Starbase, Texas. With two launch sites, SpaceX will have the pieces in place to take the next leap with Starship.
The Starship refueling demonstration has slipped two years since late 2024, effectively a day-for-day delay as SpaceX ironed out technical problems with the vehicle. SpaceX may have turned a corner with Saturday’s first-ever catch of Starship at the launch tower.
Other Starship lander tests are coming next year. The first will be NASA’s Artemis III mission, followed by an uncrewed Starship landing demonstration on the Moon. The former requires no orbital refueling, and the latter will need heaps of it.
Ars recently spoke with Steve Creech, the program manager for NASA’s Human Landing System. In this role, Creech oversees NASA’s contracts with SpaceX and Blue Origin to develop crew-rated lunar landers for Artemis.
Artist’s illustration of Starship and Orion docked in low-Earth orbit.
Credit:
NASA/SpaceX
Artist’s illustration of Starship and Orion docked in low-Earth orbit.
Credit:
NASA/SpaceX
Different landers, different priorities
For Artemis III, NASA will launch a four-person crew to low-Earth orbit on a Space Launch System rocket and an Orion spacecraft. Orion will first dock with Blue Origin’s Blue Moon lander for two days of tests, following its launch on a New Glenn rocket. The astronauts will open hatches and enter Blue Moon’s pressurized crew cabin to test the vehicle’s environmental control and life support systems.
Then, the astronauts will return to Orion and undock from Blue Moon to set up for a rendezvous and docking with SpaceX’s Starship in a slightly lower orbit, keeping it below most of SpaceX’s Starlink constellation. Orion will stay attached to Starship for just two hours, and the astronauts won’t enter the SpaceX vehicle.

title: Banks Have Had It Up to Here With Your AI Agent
summary: Major US financial institutions are banning third-party bots from logging into your accounts—and warning that any costly bot mistakes are strictly your problem.
text:
Wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers, specifically about AI agents, starting on Tuesday. The bank’s warning to early adopters could not be clearer. “Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK,” read Wells Fargo’s new terms.
AI agents, which automate online tasks and click on your behalf, have stumbled through 2026. They remain nascent technology, but a growing subset of power users latched onto the personal bots this year. Sometimes these early adopters enjoyed the efficient help of automation, and other times they publicly embarrassed themselves when the AI agents made major mistakes, like posting bank details for everyone at work to see.
Builders of these AI tools often market agents as the ultimate tool for shopping decisions, whether that’s putting together a grocery order, finding accommodations for a vacation, or discovering specific holiday gifts for your parents. I’ve used an agent to help shop for a new couch, comparing options within a specific budget and tracking price drops.
Some users value these agents so much that they are oblivious to the overarching security concerns, pairing account credentials and granting permissions for the agents to take sweeping actions without forethought. Although the segment of online transactions completed by these autonomous tools remains minuscule, US-based banking institutions are already sick of third-party AI agents.
It’s not just banks; AI agents are igniting turf wars around the web. Amazon, one of the largest online retailers, blocked Meta’s Muse, one of the most widely used AI agents, from making purchases on its platform. Travel companies are also pushing back—United recently announced that personal bots would be blocked from purchasing flights on your behalf.
As the end of the year approaches, multiple banks have enacted new policies around agents or sent warnings. In late October, JPMorgan Chase changed its terms to ban third-party agents that log in with your credentials. That same day, Bank of America warned its customers not to share login info with agents. Along with the announced change coming from Wells Fargo, Citibank and PNC have also changed their terms to include warnings about agents.
The automation, which remains a central selling point of always-on agents, is exactly what may get users in trouble. “Consumers authorize goals, not every click,” says Kacy Kim, an associate professor of marketing at Bryant University who studies consumer behavior and emerging tech. While Kim expects some consumers to feel like it's unfair to be held accountable for their agent’s mistakes, she doesn’t expect these policy moves by financial institutions to scare off the early-adopter crowd already in deep and using the tools as part of everyday life.

title: Should AI be judging our credit worthiness?
summary: Would AI be a good judge of whether you should get a mortgage, car loan or mobile phone contract?
text:
Should AI be judging our credit worthiness?
- Published
Getting approval for a mortgage, a car loan or even a mobile phone contract can rest on a credit score.
Sophie Hope was on the sharp end of just such a decision.
"When I first checked my credit score, it was excellent. But then my mortgage application was suddenly denied by the lender because of my credit report. It was a massive shock as I'd never had bad credit. When I looked into it, my score had gone to 'very poor'," she says.
It turns out, the Brighton-based nail technician and content creator, had been the victim of identity fraud.
"Someone had opened accounts in my name across various catalogue sites and ordered multiple items, including a PlayStation 4 and Nike socks," she says.
"Without me knowing, the debt was transferred to a secondary finance company. It spent three to four years accumulating in the background. It was only when I went to apply for a mortgage that I discovered how severely it had dragged down my credit score," she says.
Hope's experience shows how crucial a credit score can be, but, as in her case, it does not tell the full story.
"As a nation, we are overly obsessed with credit scores," says Funmi Olufunwa, a consumer finance lawyer and founder of financial education business, Hoops Finance.
Three firms - Experian, Equifax and TransUnion - produce credit scores in the UK, and they all work from roughly the same data.
"A credit score is backward looking. It's looking at what has happened in the past, which doesn't necessarily predict the future," says Olufunwa.
"But when somebody's looking to lend you money, they're looking at what actually is affordable," she says.
Traditional credit scoring systems also disadvantage "thin-file applicants" - young people and recent immigrants to the UK who won't have built up a credit history.
But with more financial data available than ever before - and a growing appetite for AI to make sense of it - could artificial intelligence help lenders work out who is safe to lend to?
In the US lending decisions will often hinge on a credit score from a company called FICO, which uses data from the big three credit assessment firms.
But AI-powered lending firms, Upstart and Zest AI have both built businesses which offer lenders an extra option when it comes to assessing a client's credit worthiness.
"Thanks to our machine-learning models that look at more than 2,500 variables, we believe we can make significantly more loans at low prices to borrowers from every demographic group," Upstart said in statement.
Mortgage expert and founder and CEO of The Mortgage Mum, Sarah Tucker says: "AI has the potential to help lenders analyse much broader sets of information, identify patterns more quickly and build a more individual picture of someone's affordability and risk."
If technology allows lenders to understand so-called thin-file applicants better, rather than simply applying increasingly rigid rules, Tucker believes there is "a real opportuni
